waves.title: How Retirement Villages Make Money: The Operator Model in the UK, Australia and New Zealand
waves.keywords: how do retirement villages make money, retirement village business model, retirement village operator revenue, deferred management fee operator, integrated retirement community business model
waves.brief: The title's position piece and the most winnable pillar query in the vertical: the SERP for 'retirement village business model, how do operators make money' is held by an NZ broker (Craigs), a Stuff opinion column, an Australian consumer site, a Retirement Commission page and two content farms (BusinessDojo, FasterCapital). No trade publisher ranks. Write the definitive operator-side explainer, for a developer, investor or operator finance director, never for a resident. Structure: the three revenue lines every model is built from (the development margin on first sale, the recurring service charge or weekly fee, and the deferred or event fee on exit or resale), then how each market combines them: the UK (leasehold sale, event fees, and increasingly rental), Australia and New Zealand (licence to occupy or occupation right, deferred management fee, resale gains), and the US contrast (rental and entrance-fee CCRCs, operator-owned stock). Explain why the resale cycle, not the first sale, is where a mature operator earns, and why the UK's 0.6 per cent penetration is the investment thesis every UK operator repeats. A comparison table: market, tenure, the three revenue lines, who carries resale risk. FAQ for professionals: why DMF operators report unrealised development and resale gains, why rental models are growing, what regulators are changing. The operator rule and the no-advice rule apply throughout: explain the fee from the operator's P&L, never tell a resident whether a village is worth it. SOURCE ANCHORS (pre-verified 18 Sep 2026; cite in text, do not re-derive): ARCO's key sector facts page states around 70,000 integrated retirement community units in the UK housing just over 90,000 older people, only 0.6 per cent of over-65s living in IRCs against at least 5 to 6 per cent in New Zealand, Australia and the US, and a sector aim of homes for 250,000 older people by 2030; ARCO says meeting that aim would mean over 70 billion pounds of turnover and 40 billion of investment. Those two money figures are ARCO advocacy projections: attribute them to ARCO as its own projection, never state them in our voice. New Zealand currently requires operators to repay a departing resident within 12 months, and on 18 Sep 2026 Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka proposed a nine-month maximum with 10 per cent within four weeks (RNZ, 18 Sep 2026); a three-month rule was modelled at 3.2 to 4.1 billion NZ dollars of extra capital for the sector. Do not state any DMF percentage, entry price or margin as typical unless it is quoted from a named operator's published annual report or fee page with a link. STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENTS: the phrase 'how retirement villages make money' in the first paragraph; the comparison table; outbound links to ARCO, the NZ Retirement Commission and at least one listed operator's investor page.

waves.title: C2 or C3: The Use Class Question for Retirement Developers
waves.keywords: C2 or C3 use class retirement, C2 use class extra care, retirement community planning use class, C2 C3 affordable housing CIL, integrated retirement community planning
waves.brief: The SERP for 'C2 or C3 use class retirement community planning' is law firms only: HCR Law, The Planner, Bevan Brittan, Local Government Lawyer, Pinsent Masons, Travers Smith and Cornerstone Barristers. No publisher. Write the developer's and land director's guide, neutral and link-rich, so the law firms cite it rather than compete with it. Structure: what Use Class C2 (residential institutions) and C3 (dwellinghouses) are under the Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987; why the classification matters commercially (affordable housing obligations, CIL rates, the housing land supply count); the factors inspectors and councils weigh (level and nature of care, age restrictions, communal facilities, whether units are self-contained dwellings); the landmark case below; and what the Older People's Housing Taskforce and the government have said about guidance. Close with the questions a developer should put to its planning adviser before submitting. Never give legal advice in our voice: describe the tests and point to counsel. SOURCE ANCHORS (pre-verified 18 Sep 2026): Rectory Homes Ltd v Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government [2020] EWHC 2098 (Admin), judgment 31 July 2020: a 78-unit housing-with-care scheme in South Oxfordshire, each unit with its own front door and kitchen; both sides agreed it fell within C2, and the High Court held that a C2 extra care scheme is not exempt from affordable housing requirements merely because it is C2: whether affordable housing applies depends on the wording of the local development plan policy. Link the BAILII judgment. The Older People's Housing Taskforce report, 'Our Future Homes', was published on 26 November 2024 (Housing LIN); NOT pre-verified: the vertical brief records that the government has so far committed only to use-class guidance; check GOV.UK at draft time, and never claim guidance has been published unless it is there to link. Knight Frank's 2025 operator survey, as reported by Travers Smith on 12 Feb 2026: 43 per cent of operators named planning as a challenge and 27 per cent listed planning delays as a barrier to growth. STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENTS: 'C2 or C3' in the first paragraph; a table of the classification factors with the direction each pushes; outbound links to the Use Classes Order on legislation.gov.uk and the Rectory Homes judgment.

waves.title: What It Costs to Build a Retirement Village in the UK
waves.keywords: cost to build a retirement village UK, retirement village development cost per unit, later living development finance, retirement community build cost, extra care scheme cost
waves.brief: The weakest SERP in the vertical: 'cost to build a retirement village per unit UK' is held by consumer-cost pages (Autumna, an IFA, an operator's resident fee page, Lottie, HomeOwners Alliance) that answer what a RESIDENT pays, not what a DEVELOPER spends. Displace them with the development economics. Structure: the cost stack a developer models (land, build, the communal and amenity core that a standard housing scheme does not carry, professional fees, planning obligations including the C2/C3 affordable housing question, finance, and sales and marketing through a long absorption period); why amenity-rich IRCs carry a heavier up-front core than age-restricted retirement flats; how funding is structured (development facilities, forward funding, JVs); and the delivery context. Where published scheme data exists, use it as attributed examples only. The figure rule is absolute here: this article becomes the seed of a cost dataset, and one invented per-unit number poisons it. If no neutral per-unit build cost is published, say so plainly and explain the method instead. SOURCE ANCHORS (pre-verified 18 Sep 2026): Knight Frank's UK seniors housing market update (28 May 2025): some 6,380 new seniors housing units were added in 2024 across 119 schemes, a 4 per cent increase; nearly 8,000 were expected to complete in 2025; 230 schemes (13,478 homes) were granted full planning permission in 2024; the pipeline stands at around 30,000 homes, nearly 13,000 under construction. Paragon Development Finance provided a 44.8 million pound facility to Beechcroft for a later living scheme on London Road, Shenley, Hertfordshire: site acquisition plus 88 homes for over-55s and affordable housing, first homes due to launch in late 2027 (BE News and Property Week, Sep 2026). A facility is not a build cost: never divide 44.8 million by 88 and call it a per-unit cost. STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENTS: 'cost to build a retirement village' in the first paragraph; a cost-stack table with what each line covers and who typically funds it (no invented figures; 'not published' where none is sourced); link to Knight Frank and to the Paragon announcement.

waves.title: Event Fees: What the Legal Definition Means for UK Retirement Operators
waves.keywords: event fees retirement housing, event fees Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act, retirement property exit fees operators, Law Commission event fees code of practice, deferred fees UK retirement
waves.brief: The SERP for 'event fees retirement homes UK explained' is the Law Commission, Mondaq, the Commons Library, POST, Housing LIN, an ARCO PDF and LEASE: associations and lawyers, no publisher. The consumer version is not ours; write the regulatory-news explainer for the operator, developer and investor, who need to know what the rules will require of their fee structures and disclosure. Structure: what an event fee is (a fee payable on a defined event such as sale, sub-letting or death, usually a percentage of sale price or market value) and why operators use it (it lowers the entry price and funds the long-run service model); the legal history (Law Commission report 2017, government acceptance of most recommendations in 2019, the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 definition); what is still to come (disclosure regulations and a code of practice) and what compliance will cost operators in documentation, sales process and reputational terms; and how this compares with Australia's and New Zealand's exit-fee regimes. The no-advice rule is absolute: nothing tells a buyer whether a fee is fair. SOURCE ANCHORS (pre-verified 18 Sep 2026): ARCO's press release of 24 May 2024: the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Bill, approved in the pre-election wash-up on 24 May 2024, gives event fees a legal definition as charges 'in relation to a new lease being granted, assigned or terminated' with 'the amount calculated by a method determinable in advance'; ARCO chief executive Michael Voges called on the next government to adopt the Law Commission's proposals for a code of practice to stamp out non-disclosure. The Law Commission's project page is 'Event fees in retirement properties'. The timetable for disclosure regulations and the code is NOT confirmed: write 'expected' and 'further consultation', never a date. Australia comparison: Victoria amended its Retirement Villages Act in May 2025 to require operators to explain how exit fees are calculated, and in Aug 2026 the Victorian Court of Appeal upheld a ruling against Lifestyle Communities over deferred management fees, with up to 78 million Australian dollars in refunds (ACM regional papers, 14 Sep 2026). STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENTS: 'event fees' in the first paragraph; a status table (item, status, next step, what it means for operators); outbound links to ARCO, the Law Commission project page and the Act on legislation.gov.uk.

waves.title: Deferred Management Fees on the Operator's P&L: UK, Australia and NZ
waves.keywords: deferred management fee modelling, DMF retirement village operator, DMF vs event fees, retirement village resale gains accounting, occupation right agreement operator
waves.brief: The consumer SERP ('deferred management fee retirement village explained') is operators and resident guides and we do not chase it. We write the version nobody has: DMF modelling from the operator's side. Structure: how a DMF accrues (a percentage of the entry price or resale price building up over the first years of occupancy, capped), how it and the resale gain show up in an operator's accounts, why listed AU/NZ operators report fair-value gains alongside underlying profit, the cash-flow timing problem (the DMF is collected only when the unit resells, which is why repayment deadlines matter), and how the UK event fee differs (a lease event, typically calculated on sale). Then the regulatory squeeze in all three markets and what it does to the model. A table comparing the UK event fee, the NZ occupation right agreement DMF and the Australian DMF: legal basis, when it is payable, who carries resale risk, current regulatory change. Every percentage must come from a named operator's published document with a link, or it does not appear. The no-advice rule applies absolutely: this is for finance directors and investors. SOURCE ANCHORS (pre-verified 18 Sep 2026): NZ proposal of 18 Sep 2026 (Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka, reported by RNZ): maximum repayment period cut from the current 12 months to nine, with 10 per cent paid within four weeks; legislation not expected to pass until after the election; government modelling put a three-month rule at 3.2 to 4.1 billion NZ dollars of extra capital for the sector and up to 118,000 NZ dollars on the cost of entering a village if all costs were passed on. Victoria: the Court of Appeal in Aug 2026 upheld the Gauci ruling against Lifestyle Communities over deferred management fees; up to 78 million Australian dollars in refunds (ACM, 14 Sep 2026); the court reasoned the amount only becomes knowable when the home is sold. STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENTS: 'deferred management fee' in the first paragraph; the three-market table; links to the NZ Retirement Commission and one operator annual report.

waves.title: New Zealand's Nine-Month Repayment Cap: What It Means for Operators
waves.keywords: retirement village repayment reform New Zealand, Retirement Villages Act review NZ, retirement village refund 12 months, occupation right agreement repayment, NZ retirement village operators
waves.brief: The biggest live regulatory story in the vertical, and the proof of why a UK title benchmarks against NZ: both markets run a deferred-fee model. Write the operator and investor analysis, not the resident story. Structure: what was proposed on 18 Sep 2026 and what it replaces; the capital and cash-flow arithmetic for operators (the repayment clock now runs regardless of resale); the government's own modelling of the stricter option; how operators, residents' groups and consumer bodies responded (attribute each; RNZ reported a residents' association calling it a disgrace, NZDoctor reported Consumer NZ criticising it, and industry bodies have been calling for legal certainty; name each body only as the linked source names it); what happens next (a bill after the election); and the read-across to the UK event-fee regime and Australian state law. Never name a private resident; cover waits and refunds as regulatory and reputational risk to operators, per the resident-harm rule. SOURCE ANCHORS (pre-verified 18 Sep 2026; RNZ, 18 Sep 2026): Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka proposed a nine-month maximum repayment period with 10 per cent within four weeks; operators currently must repay within 12 months of a resident leaving; the government considered a three-month deadline, but modelling found it could require the sector to hold or access 3.2 to 4.1 billion NZ dollars and add up to 118,000 NZ dollars to the cost of entering a village if all costs were passed on; legislation is not set to pass until after the election. Minister's quote (RNZ): 'Older Kiwis told us the balance needed to shift further towards residents. They told us 12 months was still too long.'
